title: Do Police Reduce Crime? Estimates Using the Allocation of Police Forces After a Terrorist Attack
research_question: Does an increase in observable, fixed police presence on a city block causally reduce the incidence of crime, specifically motor-vehicle theft? Are any deterrent effects local to the protected location, or do they extend to nearby blocks?
data_description: The authors collected block-level data on motor-vehicle thefts in three non-contiguous neighborhoods of Buenos Aires (Belgrano, Villa Crespo, and Once), covering 876 city blocks that represent about 3.2% of the city's area and 6.9% of its population. The information was obtained directly from police station records and includes the address, make and year of vehicle, day and time of report, and whether the theft was violent. The sample period runs from April 1 to December 31, 1994, yielding monthly (and weekly) observations per block, with 794 non-armed thefts recorded. The authors also geocoded the precise location of every Jewish institution (45 in or near the neighborhoods, 37 inside) and constructed distance categories: same block, one block away, two blocks away, or farther. Census-fraction socioeconomic variables from the 1991 census are used to check pre-treatment balance.
institutional_context: On July 18, 1994, a terrorist bombing destroyed the AMIA, the main Jewish center in Buenos Aires, killing 85 people and wounding more than 300. One week later, on July 25, the Argentine federal government assigned 24-hour uniformed police protection to every Jewish and Muslim institution in the country (synagogues, mosques, schools, clubs, cemeteries), a policy still in force years later. Officers were reassigned from administrative posts, the Communications Division, and the Mounted Police to staff fixed positions in front of these buildings, while authorities tried to maintain prior patrol levels elsewhere in the affected neighborhoods. Because the geographic location of Jewish institutions was determined long before the attack and unrelated to local car-theft patterns, the sudden, terror-induced reallocation of police created sharp, plausibly exogenous variation in visible police presence across blocks within the same neighborhoods.
ground_truth_notes: The effect is extremely local, with no evidence of spillover to nearby blocks. Confidence is less than 1.0 due to potential unobserved factors affecting crime rates.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: One-line: DID — treatment = blocks with Jewish institutions, control = blocks more than two blocks away from Jewish institutions; shock/instrument/cutoff = terrorist attack on July 18, 1994

key_variables.treatment: Blocks that contain a Jewish institution
key_variables.control: Blocks more than two blocks away from the nearest Jewish institution
key_variables.outcome: Number of car thefts per block

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Police presence significantly reduces car thefts in blocks with Jewish institutions.
_legacy_v1_ground_truth.main_effect: Relative to the control group, car thefts fall by 75% in the blocks in which the protected institutions are situated.
